GraceChangeDesignContext.Rationale:
This bundle exists because the audit found two failures of architectural truth at the same browser-provider boundary.
The first is an evidence failure with direct runtime consequences. M1.2 explicitly required finite, testable production budgets, yet ProviderBudgetLimits contains max_contexts and max_pages_per_context without corresponding enforcement in BrowserProviderCore. The broadly named provider_budget_limits_enforcement test injects values for all three current provider limits but asserts only the input-text bound. The failure is therefore not merely missing test coverage: an applied GRACE claim can remain green while named resource-policy fields are inert.
The second is a protocol-identity failure. Browser contracts intentionally reuse operation vocabulary such as create, close and list. The native provider process currently transmits operation and payload but not the browser contract that owns the operation. BrowserProviderCore therefore recovers the missing identity by looking at payload fields even though the generic native Envelope does not require this loss of information because its payload is opaque; the ambiguity is local to the browser-provider call representation.
The findings belong together because both concern whether the provider boundary truthfully enforces what its contracts say: resource policy must be executable rather than decorative, and capability identity must be explicit rather than reconstructed from request data. A narrow remediation can fix both without redesigning the browser family or the generic kernel.

Alternatives.Alternative: Add two assertions to provider_budget_limits_enforcement without changing BrowserProviderCore. This is not viable because the limits are not merely untested; they are currently not enforced.

Delete max_contexts and max_pages_per_context and weaken the historical M1.2 boundedness claim. This is not selected because finite contexts/pages are reasonable production bounds and the applied specification already committed to bounded resource behavior. If evidence proves a specific bound belongs at another layer, ownership may move explicitly, but the guarantee may not disappear silently.

Keep operation-only native IPC and make the payload-shape heuristic more rigorous. This is not selected because no heuristic is needed: the caller already knows the capability contract and the provider already has an explicit contract-plus-operation dispatch seam.

Make all operation names globally unique, for example create_context and create_page, and retain no contract field. This reduces ambiguity but collapses a contract-oriented capability model into a flat command namespace and duplicates identity already present in the architecture.

Bump the generic worldline-plugin-protocol PROTOCOL_VERSION solely for the browser routing repair. This is not selected by default because Envelope payload is intentionally opaque and can carry a revised browser-provider request representation without changing generic framing semantics.

Remove BrowserProviderCore::dispatch immediately and accept only dispatch_contract. This is architecturally attractive but may create an unnecessary migration blast radius. The preferred direction is to make the native path explicit first, then either delete dispatch or retain it only as a bounded compatibility adapter with no payload-shape inference.

Combine this work with the active request-policy/adblock bundle. This is not selected because request interception has its own hot-path, lifecycle and policy questions. It should consume the repaired provider boundary, not obscure the audit remediation inside a larger feature change.

DeferredDecisions.Decision: The plan will decide the exact typed shape of the native browser capability request. The minimum required information is explicit contract identity, operation and payload. A contract version field may be carried directly if that better matches existing capability negotiation, but the remediation does not require inventing a second version system.

The plan will decide whether operation-only unambiguous legacy aliases are still needed by repository consumers. Any retained legacy form must map to one contract without inspecting payload shape and must have a removal condition. Ambiguous bare create/close/list forms are expected to disappear from production routing.

The plan will define the exact limit-error representation. Reusing an existing bounded/invalid-request error is acceptable if callers can distinguish saturation deterministically; introducing a new public stable BrowserError variant is not assumed and must respect compatibility rules.

The plan will establish lifecycle accounting for context/page capacity, including close, failed create, backend failure and provider restart. The simplest correct owner is preferred over a second shadow inventory.

The plan will build a finite-budget evidence matrix from the applied M1.2 criteria before changing code. Existing generic native-host max_in_flight, max_frame_bytes and deadlines should be referenced as separately owned evidence when correct rather than reimplemented in BrowserProviderCore.

Query, capture, mailbox and dispatch-queue claims discovered by the budget matrix may reveal additional missing enforcement. Findings that are direct instances of the same M1.2 boundedness contract may be repaired in this bundle if they remain bounded and do not require a new architecture. Materially separate defects require a follow-on change instead of silently expanding scope.

The plan will choose a static architecture assertion that rejects payload-shape contract inference without banning ordinary payload validation. The check should target routing ownership, not grep for every use of context_id or page_id.

The historical applied M1.2 bundle remains unchanged. The remediation may update current graph/verification projections after successful evidence so present truth points to the new closure without rewriting history.

Scenarios.Scenario: A provider is constructed with max_contexts = 2. Two context creates reach the backend and succeed. A third request is rejected deterministically before creating a third backend context. After one context is closed, one replacement context may be created.

A context has max_pages_per_context = 2. Its third page create is rejected, while a second context can still create its own pages up to its independent per-context limit. Closing a page releases one slot without disturbing the other context.

A native caller sends contract = browser.context, operation = create and a valid CreateContextRequest. The provider routes by explicit contract. Adding an irrelevant context_id-like field cannot redirect the call to browser.page.

A native caller sends contract = browser.page, operation = create and a valid CreatePageRequest. The same operation string is legal because the contract identity is explicit. No payload inspection is needed to select the page contract.

A legacy caller sends only the bare operation create. The production provider rejects the request as ambiguous, or the request is admitted only through an explicitly named compatibility form that already identifies the owning contract. The provider never examines payload shape to guess.

A caller supplies a valid payload for one contract while naming another contract. The named contract remains authoritative; deserialization or contract-operation validation fails rather than falling through to another contract whose DTO happens to fit.

The budget evidence matrix shows max_in_flight is owned by NativeProviderConnection and max_frame_bytes by native framing. The remediation references their existing saturation tests if sufficient and adds missing evidence only where the applied M1.2 claim is not actually proven.

Real Windows S2/S3B executes through the native provider with explicit contract identity and remains green. Reference tests stay available for deterministic lower-level coverage but no production proving path depends on the old ambiguous operation-only heuristic.

A future request-policy plugin adds new browser operations. It inherits one explicit contract-plus-operation routing model instead of extending a growing alias table or adding new payload-shape guesses.
